title: Build-and-Find: An Effort-Aware Protocol for Evaluating Agent-Managed Codebases
claim: Even when models all reach correct answers, the effort needed to find intent differs across models and shrinks at higher reasoning effort.
layout: 2 side-by-side dot-and-interval panels, models ranked top to bottom, cells column
description: Two side-by-side horizontal dot-and-whisker plots, titled 'High effort' (left) and 'Low effort' (right). Each shows six models as rows. The models are GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, MiMo 2.5 and MiMo 2.5 Pro, sorted by effort score from lowest at the top to highest at the bottom. Open circles mark the point estimate of total-byte R_b on an x-axis running from 1.0 to 2.5. Horizontal bars show 95% bootstrap intervals. Colors mark model families: blue for GPT, orange-red for Claude, green for MiMo, with a legend at the bottom. A right-hand 'cells' column gives completion counts such as 12/12, 11/12 and 6/12, which flag missing cells. Light vertical gridlines run through each panel. GPT-5.5 sits near 1.0 with a tight interval. The eye goes first to the blue points at the top left.
caption: Conditional inspection effort, $R_b$, on all-correct cells. Scores use the audited scoring set; missing cells are failure signals. Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals (Appendix [ref]).
abstract: Most coding-agent benchmarks ask whether generated code behaves correctly. That remains essential, but repository-level engineering is increasingly agent-managed: one agent writes a repository, and later agents inspect, audit, or extend it as working context. In that setting, a generated repository is not only an answer to a task but also a communication artifact for future work. Even when strong agents nearly satisfy the visible behavioral objective, repositories can differ in how clearly they expose the intended behavior and design choices behind that behavior. We introduce Build-and-Find to evaluate whether downstream agents can efficiently recover intended choices from generated repositories. For each task, a builder creates a codebase from a hidden specification; a finder receives only the codebase and a specification-traced question bank. The protocol separates behavioral correctness from artifact-side recovery and reports recovery accuracy, repeatability, implementation coverage, and inspection effort. Evaluation proceeds in two stages: the first uses recovery accuracy and stability as gates to establish that finders can reliably recover the intended choices; the second compares inspection effort by the same finder across artifacts that pass these gates and allow the same intent to be recovered. Lower effort suggests that the artifact makes that intent easier to locate. We find that several frontier models approach saturation in intent recovery on our task pack, yet second-stage inspection effort reveals differences among their generated artifacts, providing a dimension beyond accuracy for comparing artifact legibility. We also audit artifacts to distinguish unimplemented specification claims from finder failures and check whether correct answers are supported by artifact evidence. We release the harness and benchmark data for reproducibility and extension.
